chapters.title: Chapter 5: ESOPs from the Company’s Side

lessons.title: Designing an ESOP Plan: Pool Size, Allocation and Vesting Choices for Founders and HR

children.text: If you run a company or its people function, the ESOP decisions you make once will shape hiring, retention and cap table conversations for years. Most of them are made badly, for an understandable reason: the plan is usually copied from a template a lawyer had lying around, and the numbers are picked to match whatever an investor mentioned in a meeting.
This lesson builds the plan from the bottom up instead.

body.text: Do not start with a pool percentage. Start with the people you need to hire, what equity each of them expects, and what you can defend to your board. The pool size is the output of that exercise, not the input.

children.text: Step One: Build the Pool From the Hiring Plan
A
pool
sized by instinct is either too small, forcing an awkward top-up mid-round, or too large, diluting founders for no reason. Build it from the actual plan for the next 18 to 24 months.

markDefs.definition: The block of shares reserved for employee grants, approved by shareholders. Grants cannot exceed it.

body.caption: Bottom-up pool build for the next 18 months

cells: Buffer for refresh grants and counter-offers

children.text: A pool of about 7% now has a defensible basis. When an investor asks for 14%, you have a hiring plan to negotiate against rather than a feeling. And when the plan changes, which it will, you can rebuild the number in ten minutes.

body.title: Size the Pool
body.prompt: A hiring plan needs 2 VPs at 0.75% each, 5 directors at 0.30% each, 15 senior individual contributors at 0.10% each and 40 individual contributors at 0.03% each. What total percentage does the plan itself require, before any buffer?
body.explanation: 1.5% + 1.5% + 1.5% + 1.2% = 5.7%. Adding a 20% buffer for refresh grants and counter-offers takes it to 6.84%, so a 7% pool is a reasonable ask to take to shareholders.

children.text: Step Two: Set Bands, Then Stick to Them
Grant sizes negotiated case by case produce a cap table nobody can defend and a company where people compare notes and lose trust.
Bands
by level fix that.

markDefs.definition: A range of grant sizes attached to a seniority level, used to keep grants consistent across the company.

body.caption: Indicative equity bands at an Indian growth-stage startup

cells: Usually the only grants that materially move the cap table
Expect negotiation, and hold the line on structure rather than size
The band where refresh grants matter most
Often the highest impact per rupee of dilution
Keep it meaningful or do not grant at all

body.text: These are norms drawn from market commentary, not rules, and they move with stage, sector and funding environment. Use them as a starting point, then calibrate against what your own recent candidates actually accepted.

children.text: Step Three: Choose How You Size Individual Grants

body.title: Two ways to decide what one person gets

columns.label: Percentage based
points: Grant a fixed percentage of the company by level
Simple to explain and easy to keep consistent
Early employees benefit enormously if the company grows
But the rupee value of the same band swings wildly between rounds

columns.label: Value based
points: Decide a rupee value, then divide by the current share value
Keeps offers competitive against cash compensation
Standard at later stage and at listed companies
But grant sizes shrink as your valuation rises, which needs explaining

body.latex: \text{Options granted} = \frac{\text{Target annual ESOP value} \times \text{Vesting years}}{\text{Fair market value per share}}
body.caption: The value-based method, which is how most structured compensation bands work.

children.text: Take an engineer on a salary of ₹30 lakh where the policy is to target ESOP value at 40% of salary a year over a 4-year vest. That is ₹12 lakh a year, so a grant value of ₹48 lakh. At a fair market value of ₹600 a share, the grant is 8,000 options. With an exercise price of ₹10, the grant would be worth ₹47.2 lakh net if the share value merely held.

body.title: Size One Grant
body.prompt: Policy targets ESOP value at 40% of a ₹30 lakh salary each year, across a 4-year vesting period. The current fair market value is ₹600 per share. How many options should the grant be?
body.explanation: ₹12 lakh a year × 4 years = ₹48 lakh of grant value. Divided by ₹600 a share, that is 8,000 options.

children.text: Step Four: The Structural Choices That Decide Whether It Works
Pool size and grant size get all the attention. These four choices decide whether the plan actually retains anyone.
Vesting.
Four years with a one-year cliff, then monthly or quarterly. Back-loading looks clever on a spreadsheet and reads as hostile to candidates, as Chapter 2 showed with real numbers.
Exercise price.
Set at or near face value if you want employees to be able to afford exercise. A high exercise price quietly converts your plan into decoration.
Exercise window on exit.
The most underrated lever you control. A 30-day window at an illiquid company means many leavers simply lapse their options, which saves you dilution but costs you your reputation as an employer.
Liquidity policy.
Decide, early, whether you intend to run buybacks and roughly when. You do not have to promise one. You do have to be honest that there is no plan, if there is none.

body.text: The highest return change most Indian companies can make to their ESOP plan costs nothing: extend the post-exit exercise window and say so in the offer conversation. Candidates who have been burned before will notice immediately, and it signals more about how you treat people than any slide in your pitch deck.

body.title: The part HR owns: making the grant understood

children.text: A grant nobody understands has no retention value. If an employee cannot explain what they hold, it does not influence their decision to stay, and you have diluted your cap table for nothing.

At minimum, give every option holder: the number of options and the exercise price, the fully diluted share count so they can compute a percentage, the current fair market value and its date, a vesting schedule with actual dates, the exercise window on exit, and a plain explanation of the tax at exercise and at sale.
Send an updated statement at least once a year, and again after every funding round. A one-page statement that people actually read is worth more than a 40-page scheme document nobody opens.
Run a short session when people join and after each round. The tax at exercise, in particular, is where employees get hurt, and they will not ask because they do not know the question.

body.title: The Cheapest Fix
body.question: A 90-person startup finds that most leavers let their vested options lapse rather than exercising. The founders want to improve how the plan is perceived without increasing dilution. What should they change first?
options: Extend the post-exit exercise window and communicate it clearly
Move from annual to monthly vesting
Reduce the cliff from twelve months to six
body.explanation: Lapsing on exit is a window problem, not a size problem. Extending it costs no additional dilution beyond options already granted, and directly addresses why people are walking away from value they earned. Monthly vesting and a shorter cliff are good changes too, but they do not fix the thing that is actually failing.

body.title: Design Decisions to Settle Before You Draft the Scheme
steps: Pool size, built from the hiring plan with a buffer, not from a round number
Equity bands by level, written down and applied consistently
Grant sizing method: percentage based or value based
Exercise price policy, and whether employees can realistically fund it
Vesting structure, cliff length and vesting frequency
Exercise window during employment and after exit
Leaver definitions, and who decides what counts as cause
Change of control treatment, single or double trigger
Refresh grant policy, and at what stage it starts
Liquidity intent, stated honestly even when the answer is "no plans yet"
Communication plan: annual statements, post-round updates and tax education

body.title: The Plan That Is Not Working
body.scenario: Farida is the people head at a 140-person Series B company in Hyderabad. The ESOP pool is 11% and nearly exhausted. Exit interviews show almost nobody values the grants: several leavers called them "lottery tickets". The company has never run a buyback, the exercise window is 60 days, and grants were negotiated individually, so two engineers at the same level hold grants three times apart. The CEO wants to fix this before the next funding round.
body.prompt: What should she change, and in what order?
body.modelAnswer: The pool is the last problem to solve, not the first. First, fix the structure: extend the post-exit window to several years or until a liquidity event, which costs no new dilution and directly addresses the lapsing problem. Second, publish bands by level and use them for all new grants, then correct the worst internal inequities through refresh grants rather than by clawing anything back, since taking value away will do more damage than the inequity itself. Third, settle a liquidity position and say it out loud: if a buyback is plausible after the next round, say so with conditions attached; if not, say that too, because "lottery ticket" is what employees call an instrument nobody has explained. Fourth, build the top-up for the round bottom-up from the hiring plan plus refresh commitments, which gives the CEO a defensible number to negotiate against the investor pre-money pool ask. Finally, put an annual statement and a short tax session in place, because a grant that is not understood retains nobody. The ordering matters: structure and communication cost almost nothing and fix most of the perception problem, while a bigger pool alone would simply dilute the founders and change nothing.

points: Build the pool from the hiring plan and add a buffer. The 62-hire plan here needed 5.7%, or 6.84% with a 20% buffer.
Use equity bands by level so grants stay consistent and defensible.
Percentage-based sizing suits early stage; value-based sizing suits later stage and structured compensation bands.
A ₹30 lakh salary at a 40% ESOP ratio over four years is ₹48 lakh of grant value, which is 8,000 options at a ₹600 share value.
Vesting structure, exercise price, exit window and liquidity intent decide whether the plan retains anyone.
Extending the post-exit exercise window is the cheapest meaningful improvement most Indian companies can make.
A grant nobody understands retains nobody. Annual statements and tax education are part of the plan, not an afterthought.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Equity bands and pool benchmarks are market commentary rather than rules, and vary widely by stage, sector and funding conditions. Design and document any scheme with a company secretary or counsel.
